sections.html:
Tattnall is a farm-and-river county in southeast Georgia. Reidsville holds the courthouse and Glennville is the biggest town. Municipalities are Cobbtown, Collins, Glennville, Manassas and Reidsville, and Mendes is a census-designated place. Agriculture and the Vidalia onion are a big part of local life.

Population fell 10.5%, from 25,520 residents in 2010 to 22,842 in 2020, and the mid-2025 estimate of 24,376 shows a rebound. Owner-held homes have a midpoint value of $140,000 for 2020-2024, and owners fill 71.0% of occupied housing. Middle gross rent is $699. The county issued 74 building permits in 2025, and 82.3% of residents stayed in the same house over the past year, so some families are coming and going. The 28.1 minute average commute suggests many people work outside their own town.

Billing and collection happen at 108 West Brazell St. in Reidsville, with P.O. Box 920 for mail. The phone is 912-557-6736 and the hours are 8 to 5 on weekdays. The county also runs an online payment portal.

  • Tax commissioner: ad valorem tax, mobile homes, public utilities, timber, and vehicle tags.
  • Board of Tax Assessors: five members chosen by the county commissioners, with a chief appraiser directing the staff.
  • Board of Equalization: appointed by the Grand Jury to hear disputed values.
  • County commissioners and school board: budgets that drive the millage.

The assessors, rather than the commissioner, receive returns. A state levy cannot exceed one fourth of a mill. The cities benefit from the vehicle and mobile home taxes the commissioner's office collects, so ask which accounts attach to your address.

A taxpayer holding property on January 1 files a return between then and April 1. The first one renews itself at last year's final value, so a new filing is needed only for added property, improvements or a different value you want on record.

Homestead covers the house you own and live in, with paperwork going to the assessors' office. April 1 is the deadline, and Tattnall offers no local homestead exemptions beyond the statewide ones. Some county material asks for applications before March 1, so filing early avoids a miss.

  • Preferential agricultural property: assessed at 30 percent of fair market value instead of 40, with a ten year commitment.
  • Conservation use: valued by current use for bona fide farm or forest land, also ten years.
  • Environmentally sensitive and residential transitional land: current-use value, with applications taken January 2 through April 1.
  • Standing timber: no tax until it is sold or cut, then 100 percent of fair market value.

Before listing enrolled land, ask the assessors what the covenant means for the next owner.

sections.h2: How assessors arrive at a value
sections.html:
Fair market value is the price a knowledgeable buyer and a willing seller would agree on in an arm's length sale, fixed as of January 1. Assessed value is 40 percent of that, and each mill equals $1 per $1,000 of assessed value.

Assessors use three methods. Cost starts from replacement cost less depreciation and adds land, market compares nearby sales, and income capitalizes net rent on commercial or rental property. Business equipment and fixtures are assessed at 40 percent too. If you have a recent arm's length sale, hold on to the contract and settlement statement as your best market evidence.

sections.h2: Due dates and the relief grant
sections.html:
Read your statement first. Georgia treats December 20 as the standard date, lets a county switch to December 1, November 15 or installments, and gives each taxpayer 60 days from the bill's postmark before interest starts.

Mobile homes follow their own state schedule: a location permit within 30 days of permanent placement, then a return and permit renewal each year from January 1 to April 1.

One credit is not guaranteed. The Homeowners Tax Relief Grant shows up only in years the General Assembly funds it, and bills climb when the money is absent. Ask what credit, if any, is on your statement.

Once the assessors change a value, a written answer is due within 45 days of the notice date, and a late one is invalid.

Your reason has to be taxability, uniformity or value, and a gripe about the tax itself does not count. The assessors review first. If the number stands, a hearing before the Board of Equalization follows, and either side may continue to Tattnall County Superior Court. Arbitration is available instead of the Board of Equalization if you choose it at filing.

Assessors read the market and do not invent prices. If a recent contract differs from the county's number, attach it to the appeal.

A few calls early in the process keep the tax side from slowing a sale.

  1. Ask the commissioner for a statement of every open year on the parcel, including any mobile home or timber account.
  2. Check with the assessors that your homestead is on file and that any farm or conservation covenant is current.
  3. Find out whether the bill for the year of sale has been issued, and whether any relief grant credit appears on it.
  4. Give the title company the payoff figures so they can plan the closing statement.

Title companies search the courthouse records before closing, and anything recorded against the parcel has to be cleared for the deed to pass cleanly. Raising these items yourself keeps a buyer from finding them first and asking for a price cut.

Delinquent parcels go to a courthouse sale held in the Commissioners Meeting room on the second floor. An auction caps a long delinquency, so an owner behind has choices well before then.

Get written payoffs by year, and for a mobile home confirm the decal and permit are settled. Tax is charged to whoever owns the property on January 1, and the settlement statement is where you and the buyer divide the year. Any earlier balance is then paid by the title company out of your proceeds.

Bring the parcel number, your last bill and any mobile home paperwork when you visit or call the commissioner. Ask for each open year to be listed separately. If the house is rural farmland enrolled in a use program, ask the assessors too, because leaving the program early can change what is owed. A cash buyer can take a house with a tax problem as it stands and settle the balance at closing, which saves you the repair requests and lender delays of a conventional sale.

faqs.q: Where can I pay Tattnall County property tax?
faqs.a: At the tax commissioner's office, 108 West Brazell St. in Reidsville, or through the county's online payment portal. The phone is 912-557-6736 and the office keeps hours of 8 to 5 on weekdays.

faqs.q: What is the homestead cutoff in Tattnall County?
faqs.a: April 1 is the deadline, though some county material mentions March 1, so file before March to be safe. The assessors' office takes the form.

faqs.q: How much time do I have to appeal in Tattnall County?
faqs.a: Forty-five days from the date of the notice, in writing. Late appeals are invalid.

faqs.q: Does Tattnall County have its own homestead exemptions?
faqs.a: No. None are offered locally, so owners apply for the statewide exemptions.

faqs.q: Is timber taxed in Tattnall County?
faqs.a: Yes, when it is sold or harvested. The tax uses 100 percent of fair market value, and the rules cover lump sum, unit price and owner harvest sales.
